title: Credit card perks are fueling airline profitability
description:
Flying during the holidays can be pricey. So, airlines are pitching more and more specialty brand credit cards on your flight.

SCOTT DETROW, HOST: Thanksgiving brings some of the busiest days of the year for airlines. The industry is now paying high fuel prices, but airlines have a card up their sleeves, or really, their customers do. We are talking about loyalty credit cards. For airlines, those cards help balance their bottom line. NPR's Bill Chappell reports.BILL CHAPPELL, BYLINE: American Airlines made a big splash with its frequent flyer loyalty program 45 years ago. Here's part of an ad from the 1980s.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)UNIDENTIFIED NARRATOR: We invented the advantage program for frequent fliers, so all those business miles can add up to free vacation trips. We even keep track of your miles for you automatically.CHAPPELL: Within a few years, airlines were partnering with banks to issue branded credit cards, and now...JOHN BREYAULT: They're no longer sort of a thank you for flying with a particular airline.CHAPPELL: That's John Breyault with the International Consumers League (ph).BREYAULT: The rewards ecosystem has allowed airlines to become, in many ways, banks that just happen to fly airplanes.CHAPPELL: The idea is that when airlines create points, they're essentially creating a type of currency, and they control its value. Moshe Orenbuch is a research analyst at TD Cowen investment bank. He doesn't see airlines as banks.MOSHE ORENBUCH: I think that might be a tad exaggerated.CHAPPELL: But he agrees airlines use credit cards to focus on their most loyal customers, even when those customers aren't actually using an airline credit card to buy a plane ticket.ORENBUCH: The vast majority of the spending is spending that's being done outside of that airline brand in order to accumulate points.CHAPPELL: And Breyault says, in many cases, airlines don't have to provide anything in return for those points.BREYAULT: A tremendous amount of airline rewards never actually get spent. It's what's called breakage, and that's basically free money.CHAPPELL: Credit card companies pay airlines for each account, and Orenbuch says airlines also get paid when customers use perks.ORENBUCH: For example, they get paid for the lounge access that the high-end cards get, and they get paid for the miles that the consumer earns.CHAPPELL: With jet fuel costing far more than last year, credit card revenue is a bright spot for airlines. Last month, Delta said its American Express card program will bring in more than $9 billion this year. To put that in perspective, the airline predicts a pretax profit of 4.5 billion this year. Here's how Delta CEO Ed Bastian describes the relationship with Amex.ED BASTIAN: They are our No. 1 partner in the world, and we are theirs.CHAPPELL: And the programs keep evolving. Volodymyr Bilotkach is an associate professor of aviation management at Purdue University.VOLODYMYR BILOTKACH: With American Airlines, if you buy the basic economy fare now, you don't get any points whatsoever.CHAPPELL: Airlines get more revenue by unbundling services that used to be automatic, like checking a bag or choosing a seat. Then they treat those services as perks to reward status.BILOTKACH: There is this kind of increasing differentiation between frequent and occasional fliers.CHAPPELL: Consumer advocates say there are problems with the system. Airlines could simply devalue their points, for instance. Bilotkach says there are other risks.BILOTKACH: As with any other credit card, you have to use your common sense.CHAPPELL: He says you shouldn't pay high fees or overspend just to chase airline status. Bill Chappell, NPR News. Copyright © 2026 NPR. All rights reserved. Visit our website terms of use and permissions pages at www.npr.org for further information.
